Vascular plants. These plants possess specialized conducting tissues called xylem and phloem, which allow them to transport water, minerals, and organic compounds efficiently throughout their bodies. This innovation completely changed what plants could do. It allowed vascular plants to grow tall, with roots deep in the soil and shoots reaching upward toward sunlight, unconstrained by the diffusion limits that trap non-vascular plants.

The evolution of xylem and phloem enabled three major groups to flourish: pterophytes, which are ferns and their allies and reproduce by spores; gymnosperms, which include conifers and cycads and produce naked seeds; and angiosperms, the flowering plants, which produce seeds enclosed in fruits. These three groups comprise the vast majority of living plant species you see today.

Vascular plants have true roots, which are modified for absorption, and true stems, modified for support and conduction. This is very different from non-vascular plants with their rhizoids and lack of true roots. Vascular plants can be herbaceous, with soft short-lived stems, or woody, with hard long-lived stems that show secondary growth year after year.

The evolution of vascular tissue also enabled the development of lignin, an organic polymer that reinforces cell walls and provides mechanical strength to the plant. This is what gives wood its durability and strength. With the ability to transport water and minerals through dedicated tissue, vascular plants could grow tall and compete for light in ways that non-vascular bryophytes simply cannot match. They spread from the first pterophytes, which were the earliest vascular plants to evolve and colonize land, all the way to the gymnosperms and then the flowering plants that now dominate most terrestrial ecosystems.
